title: Enteric Fevers
path: Prevention and Control of Communicable Diseases

headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Enteric Fevers
headings.content: Enteric fevers, primarily comprising typhoid and paratyphoid fevers, represent a major group of systemic infections that continue to pose significant public health challenges in developing regions, including Nigeria. These fevers are acute, generalized systemic illnesses characterized by prolonged fever, profound malaise, gastrointestinal disturbances, and hepatosplenomegaly. As nursing students, understanding enteric fevers requires recognizing them as classic examples of waterborne and foodborne diseases that thrive where sanitation infrastructure is suboptimal. The causative organisms systematically invade the reticuloendothelial system, leading to a prolonged clinical course if not promptly identified and managed. In clinical practice, recognizing the insidious onset of symptoms is vital for early intervention. Unlike many acute respiratory or localized bacterial infections, enteric fevers present with a stepwise climbing fever and relative bradycardia, which are clinical hallmarks that set them apart. The disease burden falls disproportionately on school-aged children and young adults, making community awareness, prompt clinical diagnosis, and rigorous nursing assessments essential components of holistic patient care in Nigerian healthcare settings. Effective management begins with a solid foundation in the definition, systemic nature, and epidemiological context of these invasive bacterial infections.

headings.title: Causative Agents and the Chain of Transmission
headings.content: Enteric fevers are caused predominantly by specific human-adapted serovars of Salmonella enterica. Typhoid fever is caused by Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi, while paratyphoid fever is caused by Salmonella enterica serovars Paratyphi A, B, or C. Humans serve as the only natural reservoir and definitive host for these pathogens, meaning transmission occurs exclusively via the fecal-oral route. This happens primarily through the ingestion of food or water contaminated by the feces or urine of infected individuals or chronic asymptomatic carriers. Understanding the chain of transmission is fundamental for nursing students and public health nurses. The chain begins with the infectious agent (Salmonella Typhi/Paratyphi) residing in a human reservoir. The organism is shed in stool and spreads through poor hand hygiene, contaminated municipal water supplies, unwashed fruits and vegetables fertilized with human waste, or handling food with unwashed hands by food handlers who may be chronic carriers. Once ingested, the bacteria must survive the acidic environment of the stomach to reach the small intestine, where they establish infection. Breaking this chain requires robust infection prevention measures, such as proper sewage disposal, ensuring access to potable drinking water, enforcing strict personal hygiene among food vendors, and rigorous handwashing before eating or preparing meals.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Clinical Manifestations
headings.content: The pathophysiology of enteric fevers begins when viable bacteria survive gastric acid and penetrate the mucosal epithelial cells of the small intestine, specifically targeting the Peyer's patches in the terminal ileum. Once inside, they are engulfed by macrophages and transported through the lymphatic system to the mesenteric lymph nodes, eventually entering the thoracic duct and the bloodstream, resulting in primary transient bacteremia. From the bloodstream, the bacteria seed the reticuloendothelial system, including the liver, spleen, bone marrow, and gall bladder. After an incubation period typically lasting between 7 to 14 days, the bacteria multiply and re-enter the bloodstream, triggering sustained secondary bacteremia and the onset of clinical manifestations. Clinical signs evolve in distinct phases across the weeks of illness. During the first week, patients experience a gradually rising fever, severe headache, malaise, anorexia, and relative bradycardia. By the second week, abdominal pain, hepatosplenomegaly, and 'rose spots'—faint, blanching erythematous macules on the trunk—may appear, alongside high, sustained fever. In the third week, if untreated, severe systemic toxicity, delirium (the 'typhoid state'), intestinal hemorrhage, and bowel perforation can manifest due to necrosis and sloughing of the hyperplastic Peyer's patches. Nurses must understand these pathological milestones to anticipate complications and monitor patients closely.

headings.title: Diagnostic Evaluation and Laboratory Investigations
headings.content: Accurate diagnosis of enteric fevers requires a combination of clinical assessment and specific laboratory investigations. Because the clinical presentation mimics other tropical febrile illnesses such as malaria, dengue, and leptospirosis, laboratory confirmation is vital. Blood culture remains the gold standard for diagnosis, especially during the first week of illness when bacteremia is highest. As the disease progresses into the second and third weeks, the sensitivity of blood cultures decreases, whereas stool and urine cultures become increasingly useful for identifying the pathogen. The Widal test is a traditional serological assay that measures agglutinating antibodies against O (somatic) and H (flagellar) antigens of Salmonella Typhi. While widely used in resource-limited settings due to its low cost, nurses and healthcare providers must interpret Widal test results cautiously because cross-reactivity, previous vaccinations, or past infections can yield false positives. Newer diagnostic modalities, such as rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) detecting IgM antibodies and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays, offer quicker and sometimes more specific results. Complete blood count (CBC) findings frequently reveal leukopenia with relative neutropenia, although leukocytosis may occur if intestinal perforation develops. Nurses play a crucial role in safely collecting blood, stool, and urine specimens utilizing sterile techniques and ensuring proper labeling to support accurate laboratory diagnosis.

headings.title: Medical Management and Nursing Care
headings.content: Medical management of enteric fevers centers on targeted antimicrobial therapy combined with rigorous supportive nursing care. Antibiotic resistance has become a major challenge globally and in Nigeria, making the selection of empirical treatment dependent on local sensitivity patterns. Fluoroquinolones (such as ciprofloxacin), third-generation cephalosporins (such as ceftriaxone), and azithromycin are commonly prescribed agents. Nurses must administer these medications punctually, monitor for adverse drug reactions, and complete the full course of therapy to prevent relapse or the creation of a carrier state. Supportive nursing care is equally critical for patient recovery. Nurses should implement strict fever management protocols, including tepid sponging and prescribed antipyretics, to maintain patient comfort and reduce metabolic demand. Maintaining optimal hydration and nutrition is vital; patients often require oral rehydration therapy or intravenous fluids due to persistent fever, vomiting, and diarrhea. A soft, low-residue diet is introduced as tolerated to minimize mechanical irritation of ulcerated intestinal Peyer's patches. Continuous monitoring of vital signs, fluid intake and output balances, and neurological status helps detect early signs of clinical deterioration. Additionally, nurses must practice standard precautions and hand hygiene to prevent nosocomial spread within the ward.

headings.title: Potential Complications
headings.content: Severe complications can arise in untreated, inadequately treated, or delayed cases of enteric fevers, typically manifesting during the third week of the illness. The two most feared and life-threatening gastrointestinal complications are intestinal hemorrhage and intestinal perforation. Intestinal hemorrhage results from the erosion of blood vessels in the base of the ulcerated Peyer's patches, presenting with sudden drop in blood pressure, tachycardia, and melena. Intestinal perforation occurs when the necrotic bowel wall gives way, leading to sudden, severe abdominal pain, abdominal rigidity, rebound tenderness, and signs of peritonitis, which requires emergency surgical intervention. Other potential complications include toxic hepatitis, myocarditis, cholecystitis, pneumonia, and neurological manifestations such as encephalopathy or meningitis, collectively known as the 'typhoid state'. Additionally, a small percentage of patients become chronic carriers, harboring Salmonella Typhi in their gall bladder for more than a year post-infection, shedding the bacteria continuously. Nursing responsibilities include vigilant monitoring for acute abdominal pain, sudden drop in blood pressure, alterations in consciousness, and abrupt changes in vital signs. Early recognition of these warning signs and immediate escalation to the medical team can save a patient's life.

headings.title: Public Health Prevention and Control Strategies
headings.content: Public health prevention and control strategies are essential for reducing the burden of enteric fevers in endemic communities across Nigeria. Because these diseases are tightly linked to environmental sanitation and hygiene, control measures must target both the community level and the individual level. Providing safe, potable drinking water and establishing reliable sewage disposal systems are primary structural interventions required by governments and local authorities. At the community level, public health nursing education campaigns are crucial. Nurses educate populations on the importance of boiling drinking water, thorough handwashing with soap after using the toilet and before preparing food, and washing fruits and vegetables safely. Food safety regulations must be enforced for local vendors and markets to prevent contamination. Furthermore, vaccination plays a vital role in prevention. Typhoid vaccines, including polysaccharide injectable vaccines and live-attenuated oral vaccines, are recommended for travelers, individuals living in high-endemic areas, and during outbreak responses, though they do not provide 100% protection and should not replace sanitation measures. Finally, identifying and treating chronic carriers—particularly those working as food handlers—using prolonged courses of antibiotics helps eliminate reservoirs of infection within the community.
